text: Dendrobium pugioniforme, commonly known as dagger orchid, is a species of orchid native to eastern Australia and endemic to the region. It is an epiphytic or lithophytic orchid with pendulous, wiry stems measuring 0.3–2 m (1–7 ft) long and about 2 mm (0.08 in) wide. The plant has pendulous, thick, green, egg-shaped leaves that are 30–70 mm (1–3 in) long and 15–20 mm (0.59–0.79 in) wide with a sharply pointed tip. A flowering stem emerges from a single leaf base, measuring 40–70 mm (2–3 in) long, and bears one or two pale green to pale brown or yellowish flowers. Each flower is 10–15 mm (0.39–0.59 in) long and 15–20 mm (0.59–0.79 in) wide, with brown striations near its base. The dorsal sepal is 9–12 mm (0.35–0.47 in) long and about 3 mm (0.12 in) wide, the lateral sepals are slightly longer and wider, and the petals are slightly narrower. The labellum is white, 13–18 mm (0.5–0.7 in) long and 6–9 mm (0.2–0.4 in) wide, featuring three main lobes, with short side lobes that curve upwards and a middle lobe that curves upwards and has three wavy ridges. Flowering occurs from September to November. The species was first formally described in 1839 by Allan Cunningham and published in John Lindley's Edwards's Botanical Register. The specific epithet "pugioniforme" comes from the Latin words "pugio" meaning "dagger" and "forma" meaning "shape." Hybrids with the streaked rock orchid (Dendrobium striolatum) have been recorded. Dagger orchid grows on trees and rocks in humid forest between the Bunya Mountains in south-east Queensland and Tathra in New South Wales, from sea level to altitudes of 1,000 m (3,000 ft). It adapts readily to cultivation and can be grown in baskets using epiphytic orchid mix or trained to grow on rock or bark slabs, preferring a part-shaded position and extra moisture.
